extracted.intended_audience: individual inventors or small teams seeking to obtain a patent in the United States
extracted.subtask_description: Step‑by‑step practical guidance for assessing patentability, preparing the specification, choosing filing strategy (provisional vs non‑provisional), assembling required documents/drawings, submitting to the USPTO, and prosecuting the application. Focus is on U.S. patents (utility, design, plant) with notes on international filing options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility / subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: You may be able to patent your idea if it is a process, a machine, a manufactured good, or an improvement of any of these. Patent‑eligible inventions must be new, non‑obvious (a function or result unexpected by those of ordinary skill in the field), and useful (able to provide a practical benefit). Abstract ideas, natural phenomena, and inventions with no utility are not eligible for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: software may be patentable if treated as a manufactured good; a naturally occurring zucchini is not patentable, but a bred disease‑resistant zucchini strain might be. Claims asserting 'free energy' or 'perpetual motion' face additional scrutiny and challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose correct patent category (utility, design, plant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether to file a utility patent (functional invention), a design patent (ornamental design of an article of manufacture), or a plant patent (new plant strains developed by engineering).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Durations: utility ~20 years from filing, design ~15 years from grant, plant ~20 years from application. Use design patents to protect unique looks (e.g., car shapes); plant patents for engineered strains; some plants may also be covered by utility patents if they perform a function (e.g., chemical resistance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / prior art search
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure your idea hasn’t been patented or disclosed already; the invention must differ significantly from previous inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search the USPTO patent database, patent depository libraries, trade and scientific journals. Use keywords describing how the invention works. Issued patents are useful because they show what was considered patentable at their filing dates, but be aware of overlooked prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelty against public disclosure and use
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must not have been disclosed in any publication or used in public prior to filing; public use or publication can destroy novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t waste resources developing an invention someone else has already patented or publicly disclosed. Keep dated records of development to prove priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get professional help when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Find professional assistance—hire a patent attorney, use USPTO assistance, pro bono programs, or a law school clinic to help draft and file the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent attorneys typically have a science/engineering undergraduate degree and must pass the patent bar. Clinics can be good lower‑cost options supervised by USPTO‑approved professors. A lawyer is strongly recommended for drafting claims and formal parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use government-sponsored assistance and pro bono programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the USPTO’s Pro Se Assistance program or state and nonprofit pro bono programs to get free or low‑cost help starting and assembling documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pro Se Assistance appointments are available at the USPTO in Alexandria, VA; some programs require an initial assessment of eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for patent scams
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of services that ask for large upfront fees, refuse to put terms in writing, or try to take your idea without guaranteeing services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals of scams include pressure for upfront payment, avoiding written contracts, requesting money via phone/email, and reluctance to sign definitive agreements. Have contracts reviewed by a lawyer and check reputations before paying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide application type: provisional vs non‑provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose whether to file a provisional patent application (PPA) to reserve a filing date for up to one year, or a non‑provisional (regular) application that begins examination toward grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPA: less expensive, less complex, no enforceable protection, requires fee (~$70–$280 for micro/small entities), a detailed enabling description, and basic drawings; preserves priority for 12 months. Non‑provisional: leads to enforceable patent (if granted) and requires full disclosure enabling others to practice the invention and properly drafted claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing strategy considerations (timing, priority, international)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose strategy based on need for immediate protection, readiness to claim, and geographic coverage desires (e.g., PCT, EU filings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a PPA can buy time while securing funding. There is no single 'international patent'—apply in each country or use PCT/EU routes to simplify multi‑country filings. Expedited examination exists but is typically expensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete required application sections / cover sheet
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the application includes all required parts: title, abstract, detailed description, claims, drawings, and any other required information in the correct order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are specific rules about each required part and the order in which they must appear (see MPEP §601). Have an attorney review the assembled application before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare a full specification (narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a specification that describes the type of invention, prior iterations, the invention’s purpose, how it is assembled, and how it works; include claims and an abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must enable others to carry out the invention and disclose the best mode known at filing. The claims within the specification are often the most important and difficult part; professional counsel is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft clear independent and dependent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be written (often as sentence fragments) to succinctly describe the invention; independent claims state the broad invention, dependent claims refine or narrow them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example independent claim: 'A bag closure comprising a flat body of material having a lead‑in notch...'. Dependent claim example: 'The bag closure recited in claim one, where said bag closure is made of flexible plastic.' Sometimes dependent claims must be merged to form a new, narrower independent claim to obtain patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare technical drawings to support the disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Include technical drawings that show how the invention works and emphasize elements that strengthen the patent case; design patent drawings should emphasize ornamental aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Almost every patent requires drawings. Use a patent drafts person if not skilled in technical drawing ($75–$150 per sheet typical). Draftspeople know government drawing specifications and will highlight elements (e.g., energy efficiency components) that support patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include required oath or declaration
rubrics_metrics.description: Every patent application requires an inventor’s oath or a sworn declaration stating who created the invention; it must be signed and notarized (or a sworn declaration may substitute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making a false declaration is a felony; the two‑page oath form is available online. Ensure the declaration is properly completed to avoid formal defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose submission method and follow form rules
rubrics_metrics.description: File electronically via the USPTO website (preferred and more secure) or mail the application; note special rules (plant patents must be submitted physically).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electronic filing reduces cost and delivery risk. Mail introduces delays for digitization and is generally more expensive. For help, contact the USPTO helpline (1‑800‑PTO‑9199).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include additional required documents (IDS, declarations, receipts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a self‑addressed stamped receipt (if mailing), an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) listing relevant prior art, and the Patent Application Declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose anything relevant to your application (similar applications, most relevant inventions). Late IDS filing (more than 3 months after application) may incur additional fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay applicable fees and understand cost drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay filing, search, and examination fees and be aware additional fees may apply for extra pages, excess claims, translations, or late filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs vary by entity status (micro/small/large) and jurisdiction; U.S. filing may be a few thousand to ~$10,000; global filing can be $30k–$40k. Consult the USPTO fee schedule for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect examination delays and possible rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examination can take years due to backlog. Applications may be rejected for lack of novelty, obviousness, or formal defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rejected for novelty, consider narrowing claims. Objections may concern form; correct them. Do not continue commercialization if doing so would infringe an existing patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond properly to USPTO office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: You are typically given limited time to respond to office actions; responses may amend claims or argue for allowance but cannot add new matter without losing priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to reply within the time limit (or any purchased extensions) presumes abandonment. Responses can lead to further rejections (final). You may appeal final rejections or pursue amendments; some claims may be allowed while others are rejected—decide whether to obtain issuance on allowed claims immediately or continue prosecution on others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain diligent recordkeeping and prototypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Record everything about the invention: inspiration, why you made it, how you made it, dates, signatures, and modifications. Build prototypes where useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signed and dated records (with witnesses) help prove novelty and establish invention history. A prototype can ensure the specification enables the 'best mode' and that no critical detail was omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing follow‑on and related applications; cross‑referencing
rubrics_metrics.description: You may file additional applications later claiming modifications or improvements; properly cross‑reference multiple applications to preserve priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross‑referencing multiple applications is complicated and typically requires a registered patent attorney to avoid priority and disclosure pitfalls.
